 ‘Tis the season for holiday scams. Associated Bank manager shares tips to avoid being Grinched 
 Scammers use urgency and impersonation as online shopping increases, David DeChamps said 
 'Tis the season for scammers to take advantage of shopping and shipping. By WBAY news staff Published : Nov. 18, 2026 at 9:30 AM CST | Updated : 3 hours ago Share Add Us On Google Add as a preferred source on Google GREEN BAY, Wis. (WBAY) — The holidays are almost here, and scammers are ready to take advantage of it.
 Scammers are use the pressure of the holiday season to pressure people into acting fast, said David DeChamps, financial crimes model risk manager at Associated Bank.
 “They are fast and furious. That’s what they are looking for you to do, to make actions fast. And they create that fear,” DeChamps said.
 DeChamps said scammers are trying to make people make decisions without thinking, and they’re trying to get people to believe what they are clicking on is a good deal in a season of heavily advertised deals.
 “They’re really using the holiday season because they know people are looking to spend money, they’re out looking for good deals,” he said.
 Steps DeChamps recommends for online shopping
 Don’t click on links in emails or texts. Type in the website address or use the retailer’s app to make purchases. 
 Consider whether a deal is too good to be true. “Take a moment, step back and think about, is this really a good deal?” he said. 
 Ask someone you trust if you are unsure. 
 What banks will not ask for
 DeChamps said Associated Bank is seeing a lot of impersonation, including people posing as officials or bank employees. 
 He said that from a bank’s perspective, customers should remember one point.
 “We’re never going to ask for your password, one-time passcode, things like that,” he said.
 Scammers follow news events
 DeChamps said scammers try to link their messages to news events, including the recent bank system outages.
 “Anytime there’s [an] event, the scammers will try to link to it and use that to their advantage to create that fear,” he said. He said scammers might use events to create more urgency and fear to get someone to fall for a scam.
 What to do if you are scammed
 DeChamps said every scenario is different, but the time and effort to recover money often is more than the amount a person would have saved.
 “It does take a lot of effort if it does happen to you,” he said.
 He said recovery is harder for people who shared payment or banking information to get a deal.
 He said the first step is to notify your bank.
 “The quicker you notify the bank, the more options we have to give you,” DeChamps said.
 Sending checks during the holidays
 DeChamps said the ideal option is to not send a check.
 “There is still mail theft that happens,” he said.
 If a person has to send a check, DeChamps recommended these steps:
 Watch your account statements. 
 Look at the bank account to make sure the check reached its intended recipient. 
 Stay vigilant about checks on the account afterward. 
 “I always recommend checking your statements and looking at your bank account to make sure that the check got to its intended party,” he said.
 Talking with family and in person
 DeChamps said scam victims are not limited to older people. “It’s anybody,” he said.
 He said families can talk about scams around the holidays, including Thanksgiving, but that the conversation should be constant.
 “It’s always having that constant communication about what scams are out there, what you’re seeing,” DeChamps said.
 DeChamps also recommended face-to-face conversations when possible, such as visiting a local bank.
 “Especially with AI and being able to replicate voice or video, often the face-to-face is the best form of conversation,” he said.
 He said scams can change, but at their core they try to get a person to take action or send money fast.
